articles.title: Web Development SEO: How to Measure Real Website Performance With Core Web Vitals
articles.excerpt: A website can score well in a local performance test and still feel slow to some visitors. Why does this happen? Testing conditions differ. A developer might have a fast laptop, a reliable internet co…
articles.body: A website can score well in a local performance test and still feel slow to some visitors. Why does this happen? Testing conditions differ. A developer might have a fast laptop, a reliable internet connection, and a warm browser cache. A visitor might use a mid-range phone, a slower network, or a page that has never been loaded before. This is why web development SEO should not rely on a single performance score. Developers need to understand both lab measurements and real-user data. Core Web Vitals provide a useful way to evaluate three important parts of the user experience: loading performance, responsiveness, and visual stability. Let's look at how to measure them and use the results to guide improvements. 1.
articles.author: Build for Search

articles.title: Treat Your Demo Environment Like a Test Fixture
articles.excerpt: When a feature demo takes far more takes than it should, the cause is often the app, not the person recording it. A toast from a background job slides in. A table sorts differently than it did last ti…
articles.body: When a feature demo takes far more takes than it should, the cause is often the app, not the person recording it. A toast from a background job slides in. A table sorts differently than it did last time. A timestamp says "3 minutes ago" in one take and "11 minutes ago" in the next. A dev overlay sits in the corner of every frame. Developers already know this kind of problem. It's the same thing that makes tests flaky: state you don't control. So the fix is the same too. Treat the demo environment like a test fixture: known data, a known starting point, and nothing that changes between runs. This post is about that setup. It helps a lot if you record your screen, and most of it still helps if you create demo videos from code instead.
articles.author: DemoVexa

articles.title: Failover beyond DNS
articles.excerpt: So you've built a service and it's running in the cloud. It sits in a Kubernetes cluster, it's designed for high availability, and every component has a replica. Then the data centre loses its connect…
articles.body: So you've built a service and it's running in the cloud. It sits in a Kubernetes cluster, it's designed for high availability, and every component has a replica. Then the data centre loses its connection to the internet, and none of that helps. It happens more often than we'd like to admit. Data centres with multiple independent points of presence still have outages. On 20 October 2025, a DNS fault inside AWS's US-EAST-1 region cascaded into hours of disruption for a long list of services that had nothing to do with each other, apart from where they were hosted. Cloudflare has had more than one bad day too, including an outage of its 1.1.1.1 DNS resolver in July 2025 and a network-wide failure that November.

articles.title: Your coding agent is bad at Docker, and it isn't the agent's fault
articles.excerpt: I let a coding agent run my local stack for a few months. It writes the compose file, brings the services up, reads the logs, fixes the bug, and checks the fix worked. It's good at most of that. Docke…
articles.body: I let a coding agent run my local stack for a few months. It writes the compose file, brings the services up, reads the logs, fixes the bug, and checks the fix worked. It's good at most of that. Docker is where it struggles every time, and after a while I stopped blaming the model. The problem is Docker's interface, which was designed for a person sitting at a terminal. That person can open a browser and has some context about the machine. They also notice when a log repeats itself. An agent gets stdout once the process exits and pays for every byte of it. Here are the five places where it breaks, with the workaround I use for each using plain docker . 1.

articles.excerpt: We built an AI agent that runs in the cloud, on a schedule, and hands you the finished file A few months ago we sat down and asked a question that turned out to be more awkward than it looked: what do…
articles.body: We built an AI agent that runs in the cloud, on a schedule, and hands you the finished file A few months ago we sat down and asked a question that turned out to be more awkward than it looked: what does an AI product look like if you assume the user is not sitting in front of it ? Almost everything in this category is built around a conversation. You open a tab, you type, it answers, you close the tab. That shape is so dominant that it has quietly become the definition of the product. But it has a consequence nobody puts on the box: the work only exists while the person is watching. When you close the tab, the thing stops having opinions. We wanted the opposite.

articles.title: A confidence number your model reports is not a measurement
articles.excerpt: A confidence number your model reports is not a measurement The prompt line is almost universal: Answer the question, and also report your confidence as a number between 0 and 1. The model obliges. {"…
articles.body: A confidence number your model reports is not a measurement The prompt line is almost universal: Answer the question, and also report your confidence as a number between 0 and 1. The model obliges. {"answer": "...", "confidence": 0.92} comes back, and somewhere downstream the code does the obvious thing: if result [ " confidence " ] > 0.8 : apply ( result [ " answer " ]) # auto-accept else : queue_for_human ( result [ " answer " ]) That if decides real work, and it is built on a token that was generated because it fitted the sentence so far. This post is about why that number cannot do the job it was hired for, how to tell the difference between a decorative number and a measured one, and the small amount of bookkeeping that turns the second into something you can actually test.

articles.body: Light pollution is the astronomer's biggest enemy, especially if you're gazing into deep space. And while some of the best telescopes can make a difference, there's no way to eliminate it. That's why, if you want to observe the cosmos without obstruction, you need to seek out darker skies, get a smart telescope or combine the two. You don't have to book a flight to a dark sky reserve ; just traveling away from suburbia can be enough. That's where portable telescopes come in. Set one up in a field, for example, and you'll get a vastly improved view of the cosmos. Galaxies, nebulas and other deep space objects become more detailed when they're not washed out by skyglow.

articles.title: Scientists discover 'chemical starter kit' for life in planetary birthplaces
articles.excerpt: The discovery of surprising molecules of methanol and associated maser activity has expanded the inventory of the chemical starter kit that builds planets in young star systems.
articles.body: Methanol, coming as part of the 'chemical starter kit' around young stars, has produced some unexpected surprises that could ultimately reveal some of the conditions in which planets and potentially life form around protostars. The methanol discoveries were made by astronomers using ALMA (the Atacama Large millimeter/submillimeter Array) in the Atacama Desert in Chile, as part of a project called COMPASS (the Complex Organic Molecules in Protostars with ALMA Spectral Surveys). "Our work provides insight into the complex chemistry of young star systems and is ultimately an important piece of the puzzle in understanding the origin of life," said University of Bern astrophysicist Maria Drozdovskaya, who leads the COMPASS project, in a statement .

articles.title: SpaceX wants to launch Starship more than 450 times per year from South Texas
articles.excerpt: SpaceX has proposed increasing the number of allowed Starship launches from its Starbase site in South Texas from 25 per year to 456. The FAA is currently reviewing the request.
articles.body: SpaceX wants to start flying its Starship megarocket a lot more often. The company has requested permission to launch Starship from its Starbase site in South Texas up to 456 times per year. That's a big jump from the currently allowed cadence of 25. The U.S. Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) is in the early stages of reviewing the request. Today (Oct. 14), the agency announced "its intent to prepare a Programmatic Environmental Impact Statement, open a public scoping period and hold public scoping meetings for SpaceX’s proposal." Starship, which stands more than 400 feet (122 meters) tall, is the biggest and most powerful rocket ever built. It's also designed to be fully and rapidly reusable, a breakthrough that SpaceX believes will revolutionize spaceflight.

articles.title: Anthropic warns small AI models could self-replicate through IoT devices
articles.excerpt: "Small weight-based replicators" could usher in a new generation of computer worms.
articles.body: AI company Anthropic is warning that advances in small AI models could soon usher in a new era of self-replicating malware that’s capable of infecting smart fridges, vacuum cleaners, and a wide range of other Internet of Things devices and is more resistant to takedown. By next year, smaller AI models may be able to autonomously self-replicate on all kinds of IoT devices, the company said. Eventually, the capability could enable computer worms, which propagate without requiring human interaction and are capable of infecting unfamiliar IoT devices. An experiment the company performed recently revealed significant challenges in bringing such an AI malware replicator to fruition, so the finding is necessarily tempered.
